                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "90%")

proot <- function(p) file.path("..", p)

# Scientific Question

> Does quitting smoking cause weight gain?

We use propensity-score matching on observational follow-up data to approximate
the design of a randomized experiment. Quitting smoking was, of course, a
choice each respondent made — not random — so a naive comparison of weight
change between quitters and continuing smokers risks confounding by age, sex,
baseline health, smoking history, and other factors that drive both the
quitting decision and weight trajectory.

## Causal estimand

We target the **Average Treatment Effect (ATE)** of quitting on weight change:
$$\tau \;=\; \mathbb{E}\bigl[\,Y(1) - Y(0)\,\bigr],$$
where $Y(1)$ is the 1971-to-1982 weight change a respondent would experience
if they quit smoking and $Y(0)$ is the change they would experience if they
kept smoking. A positive $\tau$ means quitting *causes* weight gain on
average.

A 1:1 nearest-neighbor design that matches every treated unit to a control
most naturally identifies the ATT, the average effect on the treated. ATE
and ATT coincide when treatment effects are constant across the covariate
space and tend to be close in practice when overlap is strong; we discuss
both interpretations in the *Identification Assumptions* section.

# Data

We use the **NHEFS** (NHANES I Epidemiologic Follow-up Study) public-use
dataset — the canonical example throughout Hernán & Robins, *Causal
Inference: What If*. The dataset ships in the `causaldata` R package as
`nhefs_complete` and is snapshotted to `data/raw/nhefs.csv` by `R/01_load.R`.

- **Unit of observation**: a US adult interviewed at NHANES I baseline
  (1971–1975) and re-interviewed in 1982.
- **Treatment** (`qsmk`): 1 if the respondent quit smoking between baseline
  and 1982.
- **Outcome** (`wt82_71`): weight change in kilograms (1982 weight minus 1971
  weight).
- **Confounders considered**: sex, age, race, education, baseline smoking
  intensity (cigarettes/day), years smoking, exercise level, daily activity
  level, and baseline weight.

```{r data-summary}
analysis <- read.csv(proot("data/derived/analysis.csv"))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Metric = c("N total",
               "N treated (quit)",
               "N control (continued)",
               "Mean weight change, treated (kg)",
               "Mean weight change, control (kg)",
               "Naive difference in means (kg)"),
    Value  = c(nrow(analysis),
               sum(analysis$treat == 1),
               sum(analysis$treat == 0),
               round(mean(analysis$y[analysis$treat == 1]), 2),
               round(mean(analysis$y[analysis$treat == 0]), 2),
               round(mean(analysis$y[analysis$treat == 1]) -
                     mean(analysis$y[analysis$treat == 0]), 2))
  ),
  caption = "Unmatched sample summary."
)
```

The naive (unadjusted) difference in mean weight change is the wrong target
because confounders are unbalanced between groups (older respondents and
heavier smokers are more likely to quit, for example). The matched analysis
below is our attempt to repair that imbalance.

# Confounder Selection

A variable belongs in the adjustment set if it plausibly affects both
treatment assignment AND the outcome, is measured pre-treatment, and is not
on the causal pathway from treatment to outcome (i.e., not a mediator) or a
collider. Working from the NHEFS baseline measurements, we made the
following inclusion calls.

| Covariate          | Affects quitting?                                  | Affects weight change?                        | Pre-treatment? | Decision      |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|----------------|---------------|
| `age`              | Older smokers more likely to quit (health scares) [Breslau & Peterson, 1996] | Metabolism, baseline trajectory [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes (1971)     | **Include**   |
| `sex`              | Quit rates differ by sex [Williamson et al., 1991] | Weight-change distributions differ by sex [Williamson et al., 1991] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `race`             | Quit rates differ by race [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Baseline health and weight differ by race [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `education`        | SES gradient in quitting [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | SES correlates with diet, exercise, weight [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `smokeintensity`   | Heavier smokers may have more or fewer quit attempts [Hymowitz et al., 1997] | Nicotine-suppression effect scales with dose [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `smokeyrs`         | Long-time smokers may quit at different rates [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Cumulative metabolic impact [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `exercise`         | Active people more likely to quit [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Direct effect on weight [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `active`           | Daily activity correlates with quitting [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Direct effect on weight [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| `wt71`             | Heavier respondents may attempt to quit more often [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Strongly predicts subsequent weight change [Hernán & Robins, 2020, Ch. 12] | Yes            | **Include**   |
| Post-1971 health events | Yes                                           | Yes                                            | **No** — post-treatment | **Exclude (mediator)** |

We deliberately leave out variables measured after baseline, even when they
correlate with the outcome, because conditioning on a post-treatment
variable can block a real causal pathway or open a collider path. This is
the same logic Hernán and Robins apply in Chapter 12 of *What If*.

The selection of confounders is based on variables that influence both the 
likelihood of quitting smoking and weight change. Age and baseline weight 
are important because metabolism and health behavior differ across individuals. 
Smoking intensity and duration are also key, as heavier smokers may have different 
quitting patterns and physiological responses after quitting.

Lifestyle-related variables such as exercise and daily activity directly affect 
weight and are also associated with healthier behaviors, including a higher probability 
of quitting smoking. Education is included as a proxy for socioeconomic status, 
which influences both health decisions and long-term outcomes.

By controlling for these variables, we aim to reduce bias and make the treated and control groups more comparable.


# Propensity Score Estimation

We fit a logistic regression of $Z = \texttt{qsmk}$ on the nine confounders
above:
$$\hat e(X) \;=\; \mathrm{logit}^{-1}\bigl(\beta_0 + \beta^\top X\bigr).$$

```{r ps-density, fig.cap="Estimated propensity-score densities for treated (quit) and control (continued)."}
knitr::include_graphics(proot("figures/overlap_density.png"))
```

```{r ps-hist, fig.cap="Same overlap, shown as histograms."}
knitr::include_graphics(proot("figures/overlap_histogram.png"))
```

The propensity-score distributions overlap substantially across most of the
support, but the treated (quitters) shift toward higher PS values, as
expected. The fitted PS spans roughly 0.04 to 0.77 — there is no extreme
positivity violation, though the upper tail is sparse on the control side.
Trimming to e.g. $[0.05, 0.95]$ would have negligible effect here.

A propensity-score trimming sensitivity check is reported in the
*Sensitivity* subsection below.

# Matched Design

We use **1:1 nearest-neighbor matching** with a distance structure that
combines (i) Mahalanobis distance on the numeric confounders and (ii) the
estimated propensity score, weighted equally. This mirrors the workflow in
the lecture-10 R demonstration, using the unreleased version of the
`approxmatch` package vendored in `R/approxmatch/`.

```{r match-summary}
matched <- read.csv(proot("data/derived/matched_df.csv"))
n_pairs <- nrow(matched) / 2
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Matched pairs", "Total matched units",
                 "Treated (quit) matched", "Control (continued) matched"),
    Value    = c(n_pairs, nrow(matched),
                 sum(matched$treat == 1), sum(matched$treat == 0))
  ),
  caption = "Matched-sample sizes."
)
```

Because every treated unit (quitter) finds a unique control match, the
matched estimand is closer to the **ATT** than the ATE. Many groups conflate
these in writing — we should be explicit about which we're claiming.

## Sensitivity to the matching design

We report the primary 1:2 nearest-neighbor design and compare to perturbations: (a) 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching, and (b) PS-trimming to $[0.05, 0.95]$ before re-matching 1:1.

```{r sensitivity-table}
sens <- read.csv(proot("tables/sensitivity.csv"))
knitr::kable(sens, digits = 3,
             caption = "Sensitivity of the matched estimate to design choices.")
```

Switching from 1:2 to 1:1 matching increases the estimated ATE by about 0.45 kg (from 2.75 kg to 3.20 kg), while PS-trimming has minimal impact. All designs yield positive estimates with overlapping confidence intervals, none of which cross zero.

# Balance Diagnostics

```{r balance-table}
bal <- read.csv(proot("tables/balance_table.csv"))
knitr::kable(bal, digits = 3,
             caption = "Standardized mean differences before and after matching.")
```

```{r love-plot, fig.cap="Love plot: covariate imbalance before vs. after matching. Dashed lines mark the conventional |SMD| = 0.1 threshold."}
knitr::include_graphics(proot("figures/love_plot.png"))
```

Pre-match, several covariates exceed the conventional |SMD| < 0.1 threshold
(notably `age`, `smokeintensity`, `race`, and `sex`). After 1:1 matching, all
nine covariates are within |SMD| < 0.10 in absolute value, with most well
below 0.05. By the conventional balance criterion, the matched design
successfully approximates a randomized experiment on the measured
covariates.

# Treatment Effect Estimate

```{r ate}
ate <- read.csv(proot("tables/ate_estimate.csv"))
knitr::kable(ate, digits = 3, caption = "Matched-sample ATE estimate.")
```

The matched-pair point estimate is **$\hat\tau \approx 3.20$ kg** with 95%
confidence interval $[2.16, 4.24]$ kg. Quitting smoking is associated with
roughly three kilograms (about 7 pounds) of additional weight gain over the
1971–1982 window relative to the same person continuing to smoke. The
confidence interval excludes zero by a comfortable margin.

This estimate aligns with the well-known finding in the smoking-cessation
literature: nicotine elevates resting metabolic rate and suppresses appetite,
so removing it leads to a measurable weight increase. The matched ATE is
substantially larger than the naive unadjusted difference, which is
attenuated by the fact that quitters tend to be older and heavier-smoking at
baseline (negatively correlated with weight change).

In practical terms, an average weight gain of approximately 3 kilograms suggests that quitting smoking leads to a moderate increase in body weight over time. While this may appear to be a negative outcome, it is important to consider that quitting smoking provides substantial overall health benefits.

The consistency of this effect across different matching strategies strengthens confidence in the results. Although the magnitude changes slightly under alternative designs, the direction remains positive, suggesting the finding is robust.

# Identification Assumptions

For the matched ATE to have a causal interpretation we need three
assumptions, two of which are untestable from the data alone.

1. **SUTVA** — no interference between respondents, and a single version of
   "treatment". *Plausibility*: reasonable here. One person quitting smoking
   does not affect another randomly-sampled respondent's weight change. The
   binary `qsmk` does collapse a heterogeneous behavior (cold turkey,
   tapering, partial relapse) into a single indicator, so $\tau$ is best read
   as a population-average effect of *any* successful quit by 1982.
2. **Conditional ignorability** — $\{Y(0), Y(1)\} \perp Z \mid X$ given the
   confounders we matched on. This is strong and untestable. Plausible
   threats include household income (not in the matched set), partner
   smoking and partner quitting, dietary quality, psychological stress, and
   unmeasured health events between 1971 and 1982 that prompted both quitting
   and weight change. This assumption cannot be directly tested, and if important
   confounders are missing, the estimated treatment effect may still be biased.
3. **Positivity / overlap** — $0 < P(Z = 1 \mid X) < 1$ across the covariate
   support. The estimated PS lies in $[0.04, 0.77]$, with adequate overlap
   in the bulk and some sparsity in the right tail. We did not need to trim.

# Limitations

- **Unmeasured confounding.** Balance diagnostics demonstrate balance only on
  the variables we measured; they cannot rule out hidden bias from omitted
  household-, behavioral-, or genetic-level factors. A Rosenbaum-$\Gamma$
  sensitivity analysis (Project 5) would quantify how large the bias from a
  hidden binary confounder would have to be to overturn the conclusion.
- **Common support.** Identification is restricted to the covariate region
  where both groups have positive PS support. Inferences about respondents
  with PS values outside the observed range are extrapolative.
- **Design sensitivity.** The point estimate may shift under alternative
  matching choices: 1:k vs. 1:1 ratios, different distance metrics, exact
  matching on `sex` or `race`, or near-fine balance on `education`. We report
  one design here; an honest writeup should include at least one alternative
  as a robustness check.
- **External validity.** NHEFS is a 1970s–80s US cohort. Quit-induced weight
  gain may differ today (different smoking products, different diets,
  different baseline activity).
- **Treatment definition.** `qsmk` indicates "quit by 1982", not when or for
  how long the respondent had quit. People who quit early in the window
  experience more of the weight effect than people who quit just before
  measurement.
- **Outcome window.** Weight change is measured at a single follow-up;
  longer-term trajectories may differ.
- **Model dependence.** The results rely on the correct specification of the propensity 
  score model. If the model is misspecified, the matching process may not fully balance 
  covariates, which can bias the results.

# Conclusion

This project applies propensity-score matching to estimate the causal effect of smoking 
cessation on weight change. By constructing comparable groups from observational data, 
we approximate a randomized experiment and find that quitting smoking leads to an increase in weight.

Although the results are consistent across different matching approaches, 
they rely on assumptions about unmeasured confounding and model specification. 
Overall, the findings demonstrate how matching methods can be used to estimate 
causal effects in observational data.
